title: Write It Like a Pro
goal: Your kid picks one real piece of family news, like a new pet, a trip or something they just learned to do, and writes it three times for three real readers who need different things: a letter for a grandparent, a quick bulletin for the family group chat, a how-to or a story for a younger cousin. They send all three for real, then check whether each reader did or said what that version was meant to get.
need: One piece of real family news
Paper and pencil, or a notes app
Three readers you can really reach: a grandparent, the family group chat, a younger cousin
An envelope and a stamp, if the letter goes by mail

lesson.text: The same news sounds completely different depending on who's reading and what you want them to do next. Pro writers, from reporters to the people who write ads, start there. Before writing a word, your kid answers two questions for each reader: what do they need from me, and what do I want back?
lesson.before: 'We got a puppy. She's really cute.'

model.line: Dear Grandpa, our new puppy fell asleep in the slipper you left here. Will you come meet her?
PUPPY NEWS: 10 weeks old, brown, sleeps in the laundry room. Name ideas by Friday?
How to meet a puppy. Step 1: sit on the floor and let her come to you.

lesson.modelNote: Every version keeps the same facts and changes what comes first. Grandpa gets a picture and a question to answer, the chat gets the facts in one glance and a reason to reply, and the cousin gets something to do. 'She's really cute' gave none of them anything to answer.

howTo.intro: Play each reader before the real one does: be Grandpa for the letter, and scroll past the bulletin like a busy aunt. Save spelling for Version 2, and let your kid be the one who presses send or licks the stamp.

plan.what: Pick the news and the readers, and decide what each one needs (Steps 1 and 2).
Write all three, then read them aloud and revise (Steps 3 and 4).
Send them and check each reply as it comes in (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: All three versions sound the same, just shorter
troubleshoot.a: Read the how-to out loud as if you were Grandpa and look puzzled. Then ask: what does he need that the cousin doesn't?
Give it a few days, then ask kindly what they'd have needed to reply. It usually points to a missing question.

troubleshoot.q: There's no family group chat or younger cousin
troubleshoot.a: Swap in readers who need different things: a text to an aunt, a note read at dinner, a younger kid you know well.

steps.title: Pick the news and three readers
steps.why: One piece of news, and three people who'd each want something different from it.
steps.kid: Your kid picks one piece of real family news: a new pet, a trip, something they just learned to do. They list everyone who'd care, then choose three readers who'd need different things, using the Reader check card in the Writing Style Cards at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Warm up with one round of style switch: tell the news the way Grandma would want it, then the way a busy uncle would. Then help them find three readers they can really reach, and let them choose.
starters: A trip, or one coming up
A first: a lost tooth, a first swim
ask: Who would want to hear this news most?
Which two readers would want something completely different?
steps.tip: Small news works. A lost tooth told well to three readers teaches more than a big trip told the same way three times.

levels.explore: Pick the news, and point to three people in a family photo who should hear it.
levels.develop: List everyone who'd care, and choose three readers who need different things.
levels.extend: Add a reader who already knows the news, and work out what's still worth telling them.

steps.title: Decide what each reader needs
steps.why: Before any writing, your kid decides what each version has to do.
steps.kid: For each reader, your kid fills in the Reader check card: what they already know, what they need (a feeling, the facts or something to do) and what your kid wants back, like a call from Grandpa. Then they match each reader to a style card: Letter, Bulletin, How-to or Story.
steps.you: Ask questions that move them past themselves: 'Grandpa can't see the puppy. What does he need to picture her?' Help them write each want-back line as something you could actually see happen.
ask: What does this reader already know?
What do you want them to do after reading?
steps.tip: A want-back line you can check, like 'the chat sends name ideas', is what makes Step 5 work. 'They like it' can't be checked.

levels.explore: Say out loud what each reader should do after reading, while a parent writes it down.
levels.develop: Fill in the Reader check for all three readers, with a want-back line you can check.
levels.extend: Ask one reader first, 'What would you want to know about it?', and compare the answer with your guess.

steps.title: Write three Version 1s
steps.why: Same facts, three drafts, written fast.
steps.kid: Your kid writes all three versions in one sitting, each with its style card open. The facts stay the same; what comes first, how long it is and how it sounds change for each reader. They keep going without stopping to fix spelling. Messy is fine in Version 1.
steps.you: Protect the momentum: no corrections yet. If two versions start to sound alike, ask 'What does this reader need first?' and let them start that one again.
ask: What comes first in each version, and why?
Which version was hardest to write?
steps.tip: Write the bulletin first. Squeezing the news into three lines shows what the real news is, and the other two get easier.

levels.explore: Tell the news to each reader out loud while a parent writes it down, or draw the cousin's version.
levels.develop: Write all three versions, each built the way its style card says.
levels.extend: Read the how-to as if it were for Grandpa, and list everything that's wrong with it for him.

steps.title: Read them as each reader
steps.why: Your kid hears each draft through the ears it was written for.
steps.kid: Your kid reads each version out loud while you play its reader: Grandpa, a busy aunt scrolling the chat, a five-year-old. They watch where you lose interest or look confused, then write Version 2 of each and set it beside Version 1 to spot what changed.
steps.you: Really play the part. As the five-year-old, wiggle at long sentences; as the aunt, look away after two lines. React as a reader, not a proofreader, and fix spelling together in Version 2.
ask: Where did your reader stop paying attention?
What's the biggest change between Version 1 and Version 2?
steps.tip: If it sounds weird out loud, it reads weird on paper. Kids catch their own mistakes faster when they hear them.

levels.explore: Read one version to a parent playing the reader, and fix the one part that lost them.
levels.develop: Read all three, then write Version 2 of each with the changes.
levels.extend: Ask your listener to say back, in one sentence, what each version wanted from them. Fix any that miss.

steps.title: Send all three and check
steps.why: The real readers decide whether each version worked.
steps.kid: Your kid sends every version for real: the letter in the mail, the bulletin in the family chat, the how-to or story to the cousin. As replies come in, they check each one against its want-back line with the Did it land? card, then write in a notebook which version worked, and why.
steps.you: Handle the logistics (a stamp, the chat, a video call with the cousin) and let your kid do the sending. When replies come, read them together before anyone judges.
ask: Which reader did exactly what you hoped?
What would you change in the version that missed?
steps.tip: A version that missed is the most useful one. Ask that reader what they'd have needed; the answer usually points at the opening or the ending.

levels.explore: Send one version with a parent, and tell what the reader said back.
levels.develop: Send all three, and check each reply with the Did it land? card.
levels.extend: Compare how fast and how fully each reader answered, and decide which way of sending suits which kind of news.

reference.title: Writing Style Cards
reference.intro: A card for knowing your reader, four styles to write in, and a card for checking whether it worked.

items.ask: Which version got the reply you hoped for?

conclusion.headline: Three readers heard the same news, and each got what they needed.
conclusion.text: Before the next thank-you note or birthday message, ask just one question: 'What do you want them to do when they read it?' If your kid answers before you finish asking, the habit has stuck.
conclusion.celebrate: When the first reply comes in that matches a want-back line, read it out loud and say: 'You knew what they needed, and they did exactly what you hoped.'
extensions: Write the same news for a reader in the future: a letter to open in five years
Tell the news to a relative in the language they speak best, with help from someone who speaks it
Find two real pieces of writing about the same event, like a news article and a post, and spot what each one put first
Write a reply to the answer that surprised you most, in a style that suits that reader

signs: 'Who's this for?' comes up before they start writing
Their message to Grandpa sounds nothing like their text to a friend
They judge a message by what the reader did, not by how long it is
makeItReal: Tonight at dinner, ask your kid what's happened lately that someone in the family hasn't heard yet. Then set an envelope and a stamp beside their plate and let them start the letter.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

photo.alt: A girl and a boy writing with pencils at a table by a big window
photo.caption: Panama City: the same story, written from two points of view.

fromHome.text: Same facts, told a new way, is a game my kids already know. In Panama City, they each wrote the same treasure hunt in Santa Catalina, my son from his point of view and my daughter from hers. In El Salvador, they turned an informative text about the country into a song, set to a kids' tune we all knew. Both were for real readers: their grandparents, family and friends.

classroom.intro: Three real readers work in a class when they're reachable from school: a letter that goes home or by mail, a bulletin for the class board or newsletter, and a how-to or story for a younger buddy class.

tips.d: Students can pick class or school news instead of family news: a new class pet, a field trip, something they just learned. Nobody has to share news from home.
Help students choose: a family member for the letter, or a staff member if that's easier, the class board or school newsletter for the bulletin, and a younger buddy for the how-to or story.
Print one set of the Writing Style Cards per table: the Reader check, the four style cards and Did it land?. Students keep their style card open while they write.
Partners play each reader in Step 4: a grandparent, a busy parent scrolling, a five-year-old. They wiggle at long sentences and look away after two lines.
A kid can tell each version aloud while a partner writes. Most write all three from the style cards, and Extend kids ask a reader what they'd want first.
Post the letters through the school office, put up the bulletins, and deliver the how-tos to the buddy class. As replies come in over the week, students check each one against its want-back line.

classroom.timing: Choosing readers and the Reader check open the work, then three Version 1s, then reading as each reader and writing Version 2s, about 45 minutes each. Sending and checking replies happen over the following week.
